João Neves is 21 years old, playing central midfield for Paris Saint-Germain in Ligue 1, and his Defensive dimension of 2.8 already clears Vitinha's on the same radar. That number, at that position, at that age, is not common.

His GoalThreat per 90 sits at 0.48 and he has five goals from 1,287 minutes across 13 starts. For a central midfielder, that output puts pressure on any comparison. His Creation and Progression figures trail Vitinha's, and his Reliability score of 37.6 against Vitinha's 62 reflects both the minutes gap and the starts gap, which matters. But the question being asked here is not who had the larger season. It is who did more with what the season offered.
verdict.h2h: Two central midfielders, same club, same league, same system, one point apart. Vitinha's 116.4 passes per 90 and his Creation dimension tell you what he was asked to do: be the connector, the tempo-setter, the one the team breathes through. Neves was asked to press, recover, and add goals, and he did. The difference in the data is not quality. It is role.
verdict.who: Neves edges it, the harder feat at the younger age
verdict.verdict:
The VV Index gives Neves the edge by a single point, and the tiebreak is age. Producing a 63 at 21, in the same squad where a 25-year-old produced a 62, is the harder route to the same destination.

One year from now, Vitinha's ceiling is already known. Neves is still becoming it.

verdict.p1:
Cristiano Ronaldo at Real Madrid in 2014/15 was 29 years old and scoring 48 La Liga goals. The same caveat applies to his record as to Messi's: this is a pre-2015 season, and beyond appearances, minutes, goals and discipline, the rest is absent, not zero. What exists is a Reliability score of 90.6, 35 starts across 35 appearances, 3099 minutes. The efficiency is almost offensive. At 29, this was a player at the absolute centre of his physical powers, the athletic peak meeting the accumulated intelligence of a decade at the top.

His VV Score of 96 is not a consolation. It is the second-highest season in this pairing, and in almost any other comparison, it wins.
verdict.p2:
At 24, Lionel Messi scored 50 league goals in a single season. That number sits so far outside football's normal range that even now, more than a decade later, it resists easy framing. He did it at Barcelona, as a nominal striker but functionally something football had never needed a word for, surrounded by Xavi and Iniesta and Alves, yes, but finishing moves that no teammate created. The season earned a VV Score of 97, the highest the VV Index has ever registered for this comparison, and the Reliability dimension at 95.5 reflects what the raw record alone can support: he was available, he started, he produced. What the pre-2015 data cannot tell us, and the record is honest about this, is how he produced. Shots, dribbles, key passes, none of it was captured. But 50 goals in 37 appearances needs no elaboration.

This was not a peak approached gradually. At 24, Messi was already here.
verdict.h2h: Fifty goals to 48, 16 assists apiece, 97 to 96 on the VV Index. The numbers sit so close together that separating them by performance alone is not possible with the data we have. What the VV Index uses to break the deadlock is not volume or efficiency but age: Messi produced this at 24, Ronaldo at 29. The same output, the same scale, five years earlier in a career. That is the argument, and it is a narrow one.
verdict.who: Messi edges it, the equal devastation delivered five years younger
verdict.verdict:
The VV Index gives it to Messi, and the reasoning is coherent: an equal season at a younger age carries more weight, because youth at this level is rarer than excellence, and the portrait was still being painted.

But do not let the margin fool you. Forty-eight goals at 29, in the same league, in the same season format, with the same absence of supporting data, is not a lesser life. It is simply the finished version of something Messi was still becoming.

verdict.p1:
Mohamed Salah, 32 years old, carrying Liverpool's attack through a full Premier League season and refusing to slow down. Twenty-nine goals, eighteen assists, thirty-eight starts from thirty-eight appearances: a Reliability reading of 98.7 that tells you he was not just present but persistent, week after week, against every press and every plan designed to stop him.

The VV Tags speak to what the numbers confirm. His Creation dimension sits at 2.67 key passes per ninety, which for a winger asked to also score at that volume is structurally rare. He is not choosing between goals and service. He is doing both, simultaneously, at 32, in the most watched and most pressured league in the world.
verdict.p2:
Robin van Persie, in his first season at Manchester United, delivered the title almost alone. Twenty-six goals, nine assists, thirty-five starts: a striker who arrived at Old Trafford in the summer of 2012 and immediately made that team feel inevitable.

The record here is pre-2015, which means it is partial by design. Shots, key passes, dribbles, passing volume, defensive contributions: none of it was captured. What survives is the outline of a season, not its full architecture. A Reliability reading of 91.3 and the raw goal and assist return are the evidence we have, and within those limits, what they describe is a striker functioning at the top of his position during what turned out to be his peak year.
verdict.h2h: The three-point gap between 95 and 92 is real, but the comparison is asymmetrical in ways that matter. Salah's season is measured across all five dimensions with full confidence; van Persie's exists only in goals, minutes and discipline. We cannot compare their creative output, their pressing contribution, their passing volume, because one side of that ledger was never recorded. What we can say is this: a 32-year-old winger, fully measured, producing at that rate across a complete season, is something the VV Index has almost never seen.
verdict.who: Salah edges it, but van Persie's ghost makes the argument closer than it looks
verdict.verdict:
Van Persie's 2012/13 was a season built on instinct and finishing, remembered as the year he dragged a title to Old Trafford. The record honours it at 92, and rightly so.

But Salah's 95 arrives with every dimension in the light, verified, complete, and still extraordinary. Age was supposed to narrow what he could do. Instead, it found him wider open than ever.

verdict.p1:
Jérémy Doku at Manchester City in 2024/25 is a winger doing something structurally unusual: his Progression dimension reads 6.99 per 90 and his passes per 90 of 41.1 clears the pool bar for his position at the 80th percentile. At 22, with six assists and a Creation dimension of 2.06, the direction of travel is clear.

But the sample matters. 1,532 minutes across 26 starts is a part-season, and his Reliability dimension at 44.8 reflects that instability. A VV Score of 69 on thin minutes does not tell us what Doku is; it tells us what this specific, fractured season produced.
verdict.p2:
Edin Džeko at Fenerbahçe in 2023/24 was something that should not be possible at 37: a striker producing at a rate that would satisfy most clubs' first-choice forwards at their peak. Twenty-one goals across 35 starts, a Goal Threat dimension reading 1.32 per 90, and a VV Score of 83 on a 5/5 confidence card. The VV Index tagged him Goal Machine, and that tag is not decorative here.

This was a full season, not a late cameo. 2,741 minutes, 36 appearances, every field recorded. The Reliability dimension at 80.1 confirms what the raw numbers suggest: he was present, he was consistent, and he was doing it in a league that asked him to carry Fenerbahçe's weight in attack.
verdict.h2h: The 14-point gap between these two seasons is not primarily a story about quality. It is a story about completeness. Džeko gave his club a full season of goal-scoring at an age when most strikers are finishing careers, with every dimension measured and a Reliability score that held across 35 starts. Doku gave City electricity in the moments he played, but 1,532 minutes at 44.8 Reliability cannot compete with 2,741 minutes at 80.1, regardless of how the per-90 numbers look. The VV Index measured what actually happened across a season, not what a player might produce over one.
verdict.who: Džeko at 37, carrying Fenerbahçe's attack for a full season. This is what that looks like.
verdict.verdict:
Džeko's 83 is settled. A 37-year-old striker, 21 goals, full season, every dimension recorded, in a competition that demanded he lead rather than contribute. That is a specific, concrete thing the VV Index recognised and rewarded.

Doku's time may well come. But this particular season, thin on minutes and heavy on potential, was never going to close a gap that size.

verdict.p1:
Aritz Aduriz at Athletic Club in 2015/16 was a striker doing something rarer: producing at this level within a system that asked considerably more of him defensively, in La Liga, against defences that had watched him their entire careers.

His VV Score of 88 reflects a season that carries real weight across several dimensions. The Defensive dimension at 1.39 is the detail that separates him from most centre-forwards in this comparison: Athletic under Valverde demanded pressing intensity and positional discipline from their forwards, and Aduriz gave it without surrendering his goal return. Twenty goals and six assists, 2,776 minutes, and a passes-per-90 of 14 in a system that funneled the ball wide first, not through him.
verdict.p2:
Edin Džeko at Fenerbahçe in 2023/24 was not a footballer in decline finding a softer stage. He was a striker, 37 years old, producing 21 goals and 3 assists across 35 starts in the Turkish Süper Lig, with a Goal Threat per-90 figure of 1.32 and a Creation dimension at 1.26, numbers that would not embarrass a man ten years younger in a better league.

The Reliability dimension at 80.1 across 2,741 minutes tells you what the eye told you at the time: he was available, he was consistent, and Fenerbahçe built their season around the assumption that he would keep delivering. Tagged Peak, he was operating at the outer edge of what a striker his age had any right to offer.
verdict.h2h: The league differential is real and cannot be dismissed lightly. Džeko's numbers were built against Süper Lig defences; Aduriz's 20 goals came against some of the most organised backlines in European football, where the margins between a good striker and an average one are considerably thinner. But the gap the VV Index identifies is not primarily about league quality. Aduriz scores higher on Defensive contribution while matching Džeko closely on Goal Threat and Creation, which means he produced more of the same output while doing more of the work the system demanded.
verdict.who: Aduriz edges it, doing more in La Liga while Džeko's brilliance burns in a kinder light
verdict.verdict:
Aduriz takes this because the VV Index is reading a fuller season, one where contribution extended well beyond the penalty area, in a competition where every goal costs more to earn. Džeko's season at 37 deserves its own kind of recognition, but recognition is not the same as the higher score.

Two men, both past thirty, both refusing the narrative that strikers of their age belong in gentler waters. One edges it, because the water he swam in was colder.

verdict.p1:
Kroupi arrives at Bournemouth at 19 and immediately produces something that demands to be taken seriously. Thirteen goals from 21 starts in the Premier League, tagged Clinical, is not a fluke of fixtures or penalty luck: eleven of those thirteen came from open play, from a teenager still forming.

His conversion rate from 33 shots is efficient for his position, and his work between the lines, the key passes, the progression numbers, show a centre-forward already thinking about more than the finish. A Standout season at 19 in the top flight is a prophecy, not a verdict.
verdict.p2:
Kane's 2015/16 is what happens when a striker arrives fully. Twenty-five goals from 38 starts, every minute of the Premier League season, tagged Goal Machine, Iron Man, and The Standard. That final tag matters most: this was not a breakout, it was the confirmation that he was going to do this for years.

The volume behind the goals tells you something important. A hundred and twenty-nine shots across a full season is a striker dominating usage in a good Tottenham side, and his Defensive and Progression dimensions both sit above the pool thresholds for his position, meaning he pressed, he carried, he linked. He was the system's engine, not its beneficiary.
verdict.h2h: The ten-point gap on the VV Index reflects something real: one player managed a strong rate across 1,690 minutes, the other sustained elite output across 3,370, in the same league, at the same position, against the same defences. Rate matters, but volume and Reliability are also evidence. Kane's 98.5 on Reliability against Kroupi's 49.4 is the sharpest single line of separation. Playing through a full English season without dropping, missing or fading is itself a performance.
verdict.who: Kane, full season, full weight. The Standard, demonstrated.
verdict.verdict:
Kroupi's season is a signal worth watching closely. But Kane's 15/16 is a different order of evidence: full season, full output, full pressure, and he did not blink. The numbers did not thin out in February. They held.

This is what The Standard means.

verdict.p1:
Mohamed Salah at 32, in his final season at Anfield before the contract expired, produced something that defied the arithmetic of age. Twenty-nine goals and eighteen assists across thirty-eight starts in the Premier League, the Golden Boot and the top assists award in the same season, a league title to close the chapter. The Standard tag is not decorative here: this was the fifth elite campaign in a row, and it arrived at an age when most wingers are negotiating minutes.

The recorded figures place him firmly above the positional bars his pool sets. His key pass rate of 2.4 per 90 and 18 assists mark a player operating as both the finisher and the final pass, something Liverpool's system asked of him and something he answered at full volume across 3,377 minutes. Nine of those twenty-nine goals came from the spot, which matters when you weigh the tally, but twenty from open play at this level, at this age, is its own argument.
verdict.p2:
Lionel Messi at 27, in a season where Barcelona won the treble, scored forty-three goals and contributed eighteen assists across thirty-eight appearances in La Liga. The treble is the frame: Liga, Copa del Rey, Champions League in the same campaign, with Messi as the generative force throughout. The Standard tag carries the same meaning here as it does for Salah, but the honours beneath it are categorically different in scope.

The limitation is real and must be named plainly: for this season, only appearances, minutes, goals and discipline exist in the record. Shots, key passes, dribbles, passing volume, defensive duels, none of it was captured at the time. What we hold is the output alone, forty-three goals and eighteen assists in 3,374 minutes, and that output is its own testimony even without the granular evidence to show how it was built.
verdict.h2h: Salah's season is the one the data can fully interrogate: shot volume, dribble rate, duels, key passes, all present, all above the positional bars his pool demands. Messi's season is measured only by what it produced, and what it produced was the treble alongside forty-three goals. You are comparing a season you can see from every angle against one you can only see from the result, and that asymmetry is not a verdict, it is a condition of the record. One player was twenty-seven and at the apex of the sport's consensus; the other was thirty-two and refusing the decline his age was supposed to bring.
verdict.who: Forty-three goals and a treble against 29 goals at 32. The argument continues.
verdict.verdict:
What separates these two seasons is not the output but the context: Messi's forty-three goals arrived inside a treble-winning campaign at twenty-seven, the kind of collective and individual achievement that arrives once in a generation of club football. Salah's twenty-nine arrived at thirty-two, inside a title-winning side, with the full statistical architecture to show exactly how he built them, key pass by key pass, dribble by dribble, sustained across every minute of a Premier League season.

One season has the trophies and the age and the legend. The other has the evidence and the defiance. The argument does not end here.

verdict.p1:
Bruno Fernandes arrived at his 2025/26 season as a 31-year-old at a Manchester United that had been rebuilt around uncertainty, and what he produced was the season of a man who refuses to accept the narrative that the curve bends only one way. Nine goals, 21 assists, 35 starts: the Provider and Maestro tags are not honorary titles here. They are descriptions of a player posting 4 key passes per 90 and 58.5 passes per 90, both clearing the 80th-percentile threshold for his position pool and pressing toward the 90th.

That 21-assist figure is the detail that resists easy explanation. From a central midfielder, at 31, in a season that presumably demanded he carry creative responsibility across a team still finding its shape, it is the kind of output that reframes what we thought his position could ask of one player. The Playmaker tag almost undersells it.
verdict.p2:
Martin Ødegaard's 2022/23 season at Arsenal was the product of years of patient construction finally paying a debt. At 24, wearing the captain's armband at the Emirates, he contributed 15 goals and 7 assists across 37 starts, missing nothing, carrying the weight of a title challenge that consumed an entire city's hope. The Goal Machine tag earned its place here because these were not consolation goals or garbage-time accumulations: 15 from 60 shots, none from the penalty spot, with a conversion rate that speaks to a player who understands where the ball wants to go.

His passing volume sat clearly above the 80th-percentile bar for his position, and 2.2 key passes per 90 placed him among the architects of Arsenal's fluid, pressing identity. The Peak tag is the honest reading: this was Ødegaard at the summit of what he had built across a decade of searching for himself in Heerenveen, Vitesse, Real Sociedad and beyond.
verdict.h2h:
What divides these seasons is not quality but architecture. Ødegaard built his case with goals and the relentless, 90-minute presence of a leader driving a young team toward something they nearly reached. Fernandes built his with assists and passing volume at a rate that few creative midfielders anywhere have sustained, doing it at 31 inside a club that gave him less structural support than Arsenal gave Ødegaard.

One season is about a finisher who creates; the other is about a creator who still scores. The positions are listed differently on their respective cards, the ages sit seven years apart, and the context of their clubs in those two years could not be further removed. That is exactly why the Index cannot separate them, and exactly why neither of them should concede the argument.
verdict.who: One scored goals. The other rewrote what assists could mean at 31.
verdict.verdict:
Ødegaard's season holds the title push, the captaincy, the clean conversion record and the career-peak timing of a 24-year-old who had finally arrived. Fernandes' season holds the 21 assists, the 4 key passes per 90, and the specific defiance of a 31-year-old producing creative numbers that most players half his age will never reach.

Two midfielders, two different answers to the same question about what it means to be the heartbeat of an attack. The platform has looked and declined to rule, and that refusal is the most interesting thing it could have said.

verdict.p1:
Liverpool's 2013-14 season was the year Luis Suárez became genuinely untouchable in English football. Thirty-one goals and twelve assists across thirty-three league starts, carrying the Goal Machine and Provider tags in the same breath, at twenty-six years old with the whole arc of his career still ascending.

The record is thin by modern measure: a pre-2015 season means the granular data was never captured, and what we have is the headline that has never faded. Goals, assists, minutes, the Iron Man durability of a player who gave Liverpool everything. The Standard tag is earned across years, but this was the season that first demanded it.
verdict.p2:
Gonzalo Higuaín's 2015-16 at Napoli is one of the most forensically documented striker seasons in the database: 36 goals from 167 shots across 2,978 minutes, 33 of them from open play, working at a conversion rate that would flatter a player with far simpler chances. The full picture is there to interrogate.

His passes per 90 sit below the 80th percentile threshold for his position, which is the honest read on a player whose club asked him to finish, not to build. The Goal Machine tag is almost arithmetically correct here: this is what bending a table looks like, counted and verified, every duel and every dribble in the ledger.
verdict.h2h: What separates these two seasons is not the goals, it is the evidence. Higuaín's record is complete: shots, dribbles, duels, the lot, placed inside a competition and a position pool that can be measured against. Suárez's 31 goals and 12 assists in English football's hardest league exist almost entirely as a fact without context, because the recording infrastructure of the era never caught up with what he produced. One season is a photograph; the other is an x-ray. Both show something real.
verdict.who: Thirty-six counted goals versus thirty-one that still haunt Premier League memory.
verdict.verdict:
Higuaín at 28, in the season of his life, produced a figure that Serie A had not seen in decades and the complete record confirms every part of it. Suárez at 26, in a more competitive league and with the Provider dimension to his game that Higuaín never approached, produced something the data cannot fully frame.

The gap between these two seasons is smaller than the margin by which the Index measures them. What remains is the argument: the record-breaker with every number accounted for, against the one we still reach for when someone asks what pure, ferocious forward play looked like in the Premier League.
